Consummate

/KON-suh-mayt/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Consummate means to complete a deal, agreement, or marriage by carrying out its final, binding step.

After a year of talks, the two railway companies finally consummated their merger at Friday's signing.

Worked Example

The two rival orchards had circled each other for three seasons. Their lawyers exchanged drafts; their owners haggled over water rights and the fate of the old cider press. Twice the talks collapsed entirely. Then, on a rainy Tuesday, both families sat at the same kitchen table and signed every page. The partnership so many had doubted was finally consummated.

The signing that turns years of drafts and negotiations into a finished, binding partnership shows what it means to consummate an agreement.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

finalize: Finalize means to complete the last step of something - you finalize plans, a schedule, or a design. Consummate is narrower and more formal: it applies to deals, agreements, and marriages, where one final binding act seals the arrangement. Everyday things get finalized; a merger gets consummated.

complete: Complete means to bring something to an end - the most general word for finishing anything at all. Consummate is reserved for a specific kind of finishing: carrying out the final, binding step that seals a deal, agreement, or marriage. Any task can be completed; only a formal arrangement between parties is consummated.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

abandon: to give up on entirely

dissolve: to break an arrangement apart

Where it sits · how formal and final the agreement becomes — settle → consummate → ratify

settle vs. consummate: Settle is looser and weaker — parties can settle on terms informally over a handshake; to consummate a deal is to carry it all the way to full, formal completion.

ratify vs. consummate: Ratify is even more formal than consummate: it adds an official vote or seal of approval by a governing body, not just the parties themselves.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: together; thoroughly

Root — summ

Root — summ: highest point; total (Latin summa)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending

Put it together

Put it together: Consummate comes from Latin consummare, 'to bring to the total': con- (thoroughly) plus summa, 'the sum, the highest point.' Romans wrote the total at the top of a column of figures, so summa meant both 'total' and 'summit.' To consummate a deal is to carry it all the way to that topmost, finished point — the same root gives English sum and summit.

Use the root in a new word: sum

Use the root in a new word: sum: The accountant checked the sum one last time — sum comes from Latin summa, the total at the top of the column, the same root that lets consummate mean bringing something to its highest, finished point.

Word Choice

formal; business and legal contexts

In this unit, consummate is the verb (kon-suh-MAYT): to complete a deal, agreement, or marriage. Watch out for the unrelated-sounding adjective (kon-SUM-it), as in 'a consummate professional' — that sense means 'supremely skilled' and is not the one being taught here.
